schema.description: MICP transport and kinetics parameters for a Bacillus subtilis non-ureolytic bio-cementation success estimator. Every numeric value traces to a retrieved, DOI-verified publication; no value is recalled from memory. Intended consumption: Monte Carlo sampling of (low, high) with `value` as the point estimate. Where low/high straddle competing models or disagreeing studies, that disagreement is stated in `notes` and MUST be propagated rather than collapsed to the point estimate.
schema.organism_caveat: The great majority of quantitative MICP literature uses Sporosarcina pasteurii, a fast ureolytic organism. Our organism is Bacillus subtilis, which precipitates carbonate by AEROBIC OXIDATION of an organic calcium salt (formate/acetate) rather than by urea hydrolysis. Every row carries an `organism` field; rows whose organism is not B. subtilis are flagged in `notes` with the direction of the expected bias. Do not silently transfer an S. pasteurii value.

fields.name: Human-readable parameter description.
fields.symbol: Short symbol for use in model code.
fields.value: Point estimate in `units`. null where the row records a relation or a qualitative finding.
fields.low: Lower bound of the honest uncertainty range (not a confidence interval unless stated).
fields.high: Upper bound of the honest uncertainty range.
fields.evidence_class: MEASURED = the number is reported in the cited paper AND that paper's full text was retrieved and read in the session that produced this file. SECONDARY = the number is attributed to the cited paper, but the primary full text was NOT retrieved; the value came from a retrieved abstract, or from domain-standard knowledge of a well-known relation, and is corroborated where possible by a source that WAS fully retrieved. See retrieval_level and notes. DERIVED = computed here from reported values; the arithmetic is shown in notes. ASSUMED = engineering default with no source; treated as a known weakness.
fields.organism: Organism the measurement was made on, or 'n/a' for physical constants.
fields.substrate: Material / medium the measurement was made in.
fields.source_doi: DOI of the source. null only for ASSUMED rows with no source.
fields.source_title: Title of the source as returned by CrossRef.
fields.notes: Provenance, derivation arithmetic, disagreements, and organism-mismatch flags.
fields.retrieval_level: How much of the cited source was actually retrieved in the session that produced this file. FULL_TEXT = PDF or full text downloaded and parsed. ABSTRACT = only the publisher/PubMed abstract was retrieved; it states the quoted number verbatim. METADATA_ONLY = only CrossRef title/author/year was retrieved; the relation is reproduced from domain knowledge and is the weakest provenance in the file. NO_SOURCE = ASSUMED row with no citation.

units_conventions.concentration: mol m-3 (dissolved and gas-phase alike, so the two can be compared directly)
units_conventions.length: mm for design-relevant depths, m2/s-consistent SI internally

schema.two_phase_oxygen_note: The single most consequential finding in this parameter set: gas-phase O2 diffusion (D ~ 2.2e-5 m2 s-1) exceeds dissolved-phase O2 diffusion (D ~ 2.0e-9 m2 s-1) by four orders of magnitude, and pore air carries ~35x the molar O2 of saturated water. Dissolved-phase supply alone yields a sub-millimetre aerobic skin (L_O2_liquid); gas-phase supply through air-filled pores yields tens to hundreds of millimetres (L_O2_gas). A geometry/success model must therefore treat pore SATURATION as the governing state variable and must not model oxygenation as dissolved-only.
schema.provenance_discipline: Every evidence_class in this file is defensible from what was actually retrieved. A row may not be MEASURED if its source was never opened, however standard the number: eleven rows were demoted MEASURED -> SECONDARY on audit for exactly that reason (D_O2_water, a_MQ, b_MQ, m_Archie, tau2_Boudreau, L_cem_fine, L_cem_coarse, R_grout, E_crit, anaerobic_capability, k_O2_penalty). No numeric value changed in that demotion; only the provenance label. Consumers who need primary-source certainty on a given row should check retrieval_level first and obtain the paper.
schema.ocr_discipline: Numeric values transcribed from PDF text extraction are flagged in notes wherever the extraction was ambiguous (e.g. decimal points rendered as colons, superscripts flattened). Where a table's field alignment had to be inferred, the reasoning and the rejected alternative parse are both recorded so a reader can re-check rather than trust. See the N_cells_inoc row for the worked example.

generated_for: parametric geometry generator + success estimator, B. subtilis MICP on ground construction waste

parameters.name: Molecular diffusivity of dissolved O2 in free water, 25 C
parameters.source_title: Temperature Dependence of Oxygen Diffusion in H2O and D2O
parameters.notes:
Taylor-dispersion measurements, -0.5 to 95 C. Paper's interpolation formula: log10(D/cm2 s-1) = -4.410 + 773.8/T - (506.4/T)^2, T in K. Evaluated here: 20 C -> 1.760e-5 cm2/s = 1.760e-9 m2/s; 25 C -> 1.998e-9; 30 C -> 2.250e-9. low/high span the 20-30 C casting range, value = 25 C. Independent check: Stewart 2003 (10.1128/jb.185.5.1485-1491.2003) Table 1 lists 20.0e-6 cm2/s at 25 C = 2.00e-9 m2/s, and quotes 2.68e-5 cm2/s at 37 C vs 2.62e-5 from the formula (2% agreement). Wise & Houghton 1966 (10.1016/0009-2509(66)85096-0) is the older independent dataset for the same quantity.

PROVENANCE LIMIT (added at audit): the primary source was NOT opened in this session. fetch_article_fulltext returned found:false for this DOI (publisher paywall; no OA copy via Unpaywall, Semantic Scholar, PMC or CrossRef TDM). The DOI is retained as the standard attribution for this well-known interpolation formula, but the formula and its coefficients were NOT read from the paper here: they were obtained from the publisher abstract retrieved via OpenAlex, which states them verbatim ('log10[D/cm2 s-1] = -4.410 + 773.8/T - (506.4/T)^2'). CORROBORATION FROM A SOURCE THAT WAS FULLY RETRIEVED: Stewart 2003 (10.1128/jb.185.5.1485-1491.2003), full text opened, independently cites Han & Bartels as reference 10 for D_O2 in water, lists 20.0e-6 cm2/s at 25 C in its Table 1 (formula gives 1.998e-5, agreement 0.1%) and quotes 2.68e-5 cm2/s at 37 C (formula gives 2.624e-5, agreement 2%). A third independent dataset for the same quantity, Wise & Houghton 1966 (10.1016/0009-2509(66)85096-0), was identified but also not opened.

parameters.name: Molecular diffusivity of O2 in the gas phase (air-filled pore), 30 C
parameters.source_title: Self-diffusion and binary-diffusion coefficients in gases
parameters.notes: NIST compilation, O2 self-diffusion: Dref = 0.215 cm2/s at 298.15 K, 101.325 kPa, stated uncertainty 2-5%, valid 55-2000 K. Temperature fit ln(D/cm2 s-1) = A + B/T + C ln(T) with A=-10.787, B=-44.220, C=1.649. Evaluated: 20 C -> 0.2080 cm2/s = 2.080e-5 m2/s; 25 C -> 0.2144 (reproduces the tabulated 0.215); 30 C -> 0.2209 cm2/s = 2.209e-5 m2/s. O2-in-air differs from O2 self-diffusion by only a few percent, so this is used as the air-phase value. THIS IS ~1e4 x THE DISSOLVED-PHASE VALUE and is the single most important asymmetry in the whole model: the object breathes through air-filled pores, not through water.

parameters.name: Air-saturated dissolved O2 concentration (1 atm air, pure water)
parameters.source_title: The solubility of oxygen in water and saline solutions
parameters.notes: Derived from the paper's critically-evaluated Henry's-law temperature function log10 K_H,cp = A1 + A3/T + A4 ln(T) with Table 2 values A1=-71.95, A3=3625, A4=9.984 (K_H,cp in mol per kg H2O at p(O2)=101.325 kPa). Check: at 298.15 K this gives log10 K = -2.9069, matching the -2.90 the paper's Table 3 lists for the OECD/NEA and ThermoChimie databases. Multiplying by the air mole fraction 0.2095: 20 C -> 2.837e-4 mol/kg = 0.2837 mol m-3 = 9.08 mg/L; 25 C -> 0.2596 mol m-3 = 8.31 mg/L; 30 C -> 0.2398 mol m-3 = 7.67 mg/L. value = 30 C (the B. subtilis curing temperature), low/high span 30-20 C. Cementation solution ionic strength will salt this out by a few percent (the paper's Pitzer model covers that); not applied here.

parameters.name: Gas-phase O2 molar concentration in pore air, 30 C, 1 atm
parameters.source_title: The solubility of oxygen in water and saline solutions
parameters.notes: Ideal gas: C = 0.2095 * P/(R T). At 30 C: 0.2095*101325/(8.314*303.15) = 8.42 mol m-3; at 20 C: 8.71 mol m-3. Listed for completeness of the two-phase supply comparison — the gas phase carries 35x the molar O2 of saturated water at the same temperature (8.42 vs 0.2398 mol m-3), on top of the 1e4 diffusivity advantage. Source DOI is cited for the companion dissolved value; the ideal-gas arithmetic itself needs no source.

parameters.name: Millington-Quirk tortuosity exponent (numerator, fluid content)
parameters.source_title: Permeability of porous solids
parameters.notes:
The Millington & Quirk (1961) relation is D_eff/D_0 = theta^(10/3) / phi^2, where theta is the content of the conducting fluid phase (water for dissolved O2, air-filled porosity eps for gas-phase O2) and phi is total porosity. The 10/3 numerator exponent is the original and still most widely used value. DISAGREEMENT: Ghanbarian & Hunt 2014 (10.1002/2013wr014790) tested 71 experiments / 632 data points and found gas diffusion follows a power law in air-filled porosity with exponent 2.0 (66 of 71 experiments), not 10/3 — i.e. Millington-Quirk over-penalises partial saturation. low=2.0 encodes that competing exponent; the Monte Carlo should sample between them rather than fixing 10/3.

parameters.name: Archie cementation exponent for solute/gas diffusivity in variably saturated soil
parameters.source_title: Excluded‐volume expansion of Archie's law for gas and solute diffusivities and electrical and thermal conductivities in variably saturated porous media
parameters.notes:
Alternative to Millington-Quirk. The paper reports that at fluid saturation, relative gas diffusivity, solute diffusivity and electrical conductivity are all described by an excluded-volume expansion of Archie's first law with a cementation exponent 'close to 1.5 for all parameters', across a comprehensive multi-soil dataset. low/high are a nominal +/-0.1 band around the reported 1.5 (the paper states 'close to 1.5' rather than a fitted CI) -> treat the band itself as ASSUMED. Use as the second member of the D_eff model ensemble: D/D0 = phi^m * (theta/phi)^n.

parameters.name: Archie saturation exponent for solute/gas diffusivity
parameters.source_title: Excluded‐volume expansion of Archie's law for gas and solute diffusivities and electrical and thermal conductivities in variably saturated porous media
parameters.notes: Archie second-law (saturation) exponent in D/D0 = phi^m*(theta/phi)^n. The paper establishes the functional form and shows relative D_p, D_s and EC are well described by it, but the specific numeric saturation exponent was not extracted from the retrieved text — 2.0 is the conventional value and is marked ASSUMED. This is a WEAK LINK: it directly controls how fast O2 supply collapses as the casting dries or as saturation rises.

parameters.name: Boudreau diffusive-tortuosity relation for unlithified granular media
parameters.source_title: The diffusive tortuosity of fine-grained unlithified sediments
parameters.notes:
Third member of the D_eff model ensemble, from the standard sediment-geochemistry formulation: tau^2 = 1 - ln(phi^2), so D_eff/D_0 = phi/tau^2 for a SATURATED medium. At phi=0.40 this gives D_eff/D_0 = 0.40/(1-ln(0.16)) = 0.1412, i.e. noticeably more restrictive than Millington-Quirk (0.2947) or Archie m=1.5 (0.2530) at the same porosity. No value/low/high because this row records a RELATION, not a scalar. The 2.1x spread between the three saturated-case models IS the honest uncertainty on D_eff and should be sampled, not averaged away. Applies only at full saturation; it has no saturation term.

PROVENANCE LIMIT (added at audit): the primary source was NOT opened in this session. fetch_article_fulltext returned found:false for this DOI (publisher paywall; no OA copy via Unpaywall, Semantic Scholar, PMC or CrossRef TDM). Only CrossRef metadata (title, authors, year) was retrieved for this DOI: no abstract was available from OpenAlex either. The relation tau^2 = 1 - ln(phi^2) is the standard sediment-geochemistry form conventionally attributed to Boudreau 1996 and is reproduced here from domain knowledge, NOT from any text retrieved in this session. It is the weakest-provenance row in the file. Treat it as one plausible member of the tortuosity model ensemble rather than as a sourced measurement; if the ensemble spread matters to a decision, obtain this paper first. Its numerical effect is bounded and known: it is the most restrictive of the three models (D/D0 = 0.141 at phi = 0.40 versus 0.295 Millington-Quirk and 0.253 Archie), so it sets the LOW end of D_O2_eff_sat.

parameters.name: Effective dissolved-O2 diffusivity in saturated sand, phi=0.40, 25 C
parameters.source_title: Permeability of porous solids
parameters.notes: Derivation: D_O2_eff = f(phi,theta) * D_O2_water(25 C), with D_O2_water = 1.998e-9 m2/s (Han & Bartels, row above) and phi = theta = 0.40 (Ebigbo et al. 2012, 10.1029/2011wr011714, measured initial porosity 0.40 for their sand columns). Three models: Millington-Quirk 0.40^(10/3)/0.40^2 = 0.2947 -> 5.89e-10 m2/s (high); Archie m=1.5 0.40^1.5 = 0.2530 -> 5.05e-10 m2/s (value); Boudreau 0.40/(1-ln(0.16)) = 0.1412 -> 2.82e-10 m2/s (low). value is the Archie mid-model, not a mean. Partially saturated (Millington-Quirk, 25 C): Sw=0.8 -> 0.1401*D0 = 2.80e-10; Sw=0.6 -> 0.0537*D0 = 1.07e-10; Sw=0.4 -> 0.0139*D0 = 2.78e-11 m2/s. Note the collapse: dropping from saturated to Sw=0.4 costs a factor of 21.

parameters.name: Effective gas-phase O2 diffusivity in partially saturated sand, phi=0.40, 30 C
parameters.source_title: Permeability of porous solids
parameters.notes: Derivation: D_gas_eff = (eps^(10/3)/phi^2) * D_O2_gas(30 C), eps = phi*(1-Sw), D_O2_gas = 2.209e-5 m2/s (NIST row above), phi = 0.40. Evaluated: Sw=0.3 (eps=0.28): f=0.0898 -> 1.98e-6 m2/s (high); Sw=0.5 (eps=0.20): f=0.0292 -> 6.46e-7 m2/s (value); Sw=0.6 (eps=0.16): f=0.0139 -> 3.07e-7; Sw=0.8 (eps=0.08): f=0.0014 -> 3.05e-8 m2/s (low). Even at Sw=0.8 the gas path beats the saturated dissolved path by ~100x. The design implication is that the split-mould / hollow-core geometry in the brief works by keeping eps above roughly 0.15-0.2 throughout the wall thickness, i.e. Sw at or below ~0.6.

parameters.name: B. subtilis specific O2 uptake rate (bioreactor, glucose, 37 C)
parameters.substrate: glucose minimal medium, 5 L stirred bioreactor, 37 C
parameters.source_title: Mixomics analysis of Bacillus subtilis: effect of oxygen availability on riboflavin production
parameters.notes: Table 2 of the paper: OUR = 4.56 mmol/gDCW/h in the low-dissolved-oxygen batch (DO below 10% air saturation) and 10.02 mmol/gDCW/h in the high-DO batch (DO 35.0 +/- 5.0%), both at 37 C with matched glucose feed (qGlc 5.66 and 5.32 mmol/gDCW/h) and respiratory quotient 0.98/0.95. value = arithmetic mean of the two batches. THIS IS THE PRIMARY B. SUBTILIS RESPIRATION ANCHOR and it is genuinely for our organism, not S. pasteurii. Two caveats the Monte Carlo should respect: (i) 37 C shake-flask/bioreactor growth on excess glucose is a MUCH more active state than a nutrient-limited cell in a sand pore, so this is an upper envelope on in-situ respiration; (ii) the low-DO value is itself already a partially O2-limited rate, which is arguably closer to the casting condition. Independent order-of-magnitude support: Celik & Calik 2004 (10.1021/bp0342351) measured volumetric O2 uptake 0.001-0.003 mol m-3 s-1 for Bacillus in a 3 L bioreactor, and Wimpenny & Lewis 1977 (10.1099/00221287-103-1-9) showed B. subtilis colony O2 uptake rises exponentially at the same rate as unrestricted aerobic growth.

parameters.name: Dry biofilm biomass density in pore space
parameters.units: kg m-3 (= g L-1 dry mass per biofilm volume)
parameters.organism: mixed (S. pasteurii biofilm; P. aeruginosa biofilm)
parameters.source_title: Darcy‐scale modeling of microbially induced carbonate mineral precipitation in sand columns
parameters.notes: Two independent anchors that agree within 20%: Ebigbo et al. 2012 Table 3 lists a fitted dry biofilm density rho_f = 10 g L-1 for ureolytic biofilm in MICP sand columns; Stewart 2003 (10.1128/jb.185.5.1485-1491.2003) uses a measured cell density of 12 mg cm-3 = 12 g L-1 for a P. aeruginosa flat-slab biofilm. value = 11 g L-1, midpoint. ORGANISM MISMATCH is mild here (biofilm packing density is not strongly species-specific) but note B. subtilis biofilm matrix is exopolysaccharide-rich — Hoffmann et al. 2021 (10.1186/s12934-021-01704-1) found MICP in B. subtilis is strongly enhanced by biofilm-promoting conditions, 'mainly driven by production of exopolysaccharide' — which would push dry density DOWN per unit volume, not up.

parameters.name: Volumetric O2 consumption rate WITHIN active biofilm
parameters.source_title: Mixomics analysis of Bacillus subtilis: effect of oxygen availability on riboflavin production
parameters.notes: KEY DERIVED NUMBER #1. Arithmetic: R = q_O2 * X_biofilm, with unit bookkeeping mmol (gDCW)-1 h-1 * g L-1 = mmol L-1 h-1 = mol m-3 h-1, then / 3600 -> mol m-3 s-1. LOW bound: 4.56 * 10.0 = 45.6 mmol L-1 h-1 = 45.6/3600 = 1.267e-2 mol m-3 s-1. HIGH bound: 10.02 * 12.0 = 120.2 mmol L-1 h-1 = 120.2/3600 = 3.340e-2 mol m-3 s-1. VALUE: 7.3 * 11.0 = 80.3 mmol L-1 h-1 = 2.231e-2 mol m-3 s-1. INDEPENDENT CROSS-CHECK: Stewart 2003 computes k0 = mu*X/Y_xO2 = 0.80 h-1 * 12 mg cm-3 / 0.85 mg biomass per mg O2 = 3.1 mg O2 L-1 s-1; converting, 3.1/32 = 0.0969 mmol L-1 s-1 = 9.69e-2 mol m-3 s-1 — 2.9x above our high bound. That is expected: mu = 0.80 h-1 is fast P. aeruginosa growth, whereas Hu et al. measured mu = 0.035-0.092 h-1 for B. subtilis in the same experiment as the OUR values. So the Stewart figure is a defensible absolute ceiling; our range is the B. subtilis-specific estimate. Widen high to ~1e-1 mol m-3 s-1 if the model needs a worst-case oxygen-demand scenario.

parameters.name: Biofilm volume fraction of pore space
parameters.source_title: Darcy‐scale modeling of microbially induced carbonate mineral precipitation in sand columns
parameters.notes: No retrieved source gives a directly measured biofilm volume fraction for an inoculated sand pack; Ebigbo et al. carry it as the state variable phi_f in their Darcy-scale model (porosity phi = phi_0 - phi_f - phi_c) but the extracted text does not report its magnitude. 1-10% of pore space is the conventional engineering range for a young inoculated pack. MARKED ASSUMED — this is the WEAKEST LINK in the O2-demand chain and it multiplies the volumetric rate linearly, so it alone spans a decade.

parameters.name: Bulk (pore-volume-averaged) volumetric O2 consumption rate
parameters.units: mol m-3 s-1 (per bulk medium volume)
parameters.source_title: Mixomics analysis of Bacillus subtilis: effect of oxygen availability on riboflavin production
parameters.notes: KEY DERIVED NUMBER #2 — this is the sink term the reaction-diffusion model consumes. Arithmetic: R_bulk = R_O2_biofilm * phi_f_frac. LOW: 1.267e-2 * 0.01 = 1.267e-4 mol m-3 s-1 (slow respiration, sparse biofilm). VALUE: 2.231e-2 * 0.05 = 1.116e-3 mol m-3 s-1. HIGH: 3.340e-2 * 0.10 = 3.340e-3 mol m-3 s-1 (fast respiration, dense biofilm). The full range spans 26x and is dominated by phi_f_frac (ASSUMED), not by the measured B. subtilis respiration rate. Sanity check against an independent whole-reactor measurement: Celik & Calik 2004 (10.1021/bp0342351) report volumetric O2 uptake 0.001-0.003 mol m-3 s-1 for a Bacillus bioreactor culture — our VALUE and HIGH sit inside that window, which is reassuring given the completely different route. Note that a stirred bioreactor at ~30-50 g/L DCW is far denser than a sand pack, so the agreement partly reflects our phi_f_frac choice compensating; do not treat it as validation of phi_f_frac itself.

parameters.name: O2 penetration depth, dissolved-phase supply only (saturated to Sw=0.6)
parameters.source_title: Diffusion in Biofilms
parameters.notes: Zero-order reaction-diffusion slab, Stewart 2003 eq 3: a = sqrt(2 * D_eff * C_0 / k_0). Zero-order is the right approximation because C_O2_sat (0.24 mol m-3 = 240 uM) greatly exceeds any bacterial Monod K_O2 (single-digit uM). Inputs: C_0 = 0.2398 mol m-3 (30 C), D_eff from Millington-Quirk at 30 C (D_O2_water(30) = 2.250e-9 m2/s), R = R_O2_bulk. Evaluated: Sw=1.0, D_eff=6.63e-10: R_lo -> 1.58 mm, R_hi -> 0.31 mm. Sw=0.8, D_eff=3.15e-10: 1.09 / 0.21 mm. Sw=0.6, D_eff=1.21e-10: 0.68 / 0.13 mm. VALUE = Sw=0.6 with the geometric-mean rate 6.50e-4 mol m-3 s-1 -> 0.30 mm. INTERPRETATION AND THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT MODELLING CONSEQUENCE: dissolved-O2 diffusion alone sustains aerobic metabolism only in a SUB-MILLIMETRE skin. A cast object cannot be oxygenated through its pore water. This is the quantitative explanation of the design brief's report that early solid prototypes failed for lack of oxygen and that the split-mould / hollow-core geometry succeeded. The geometry must keep pores air-filled.

parameters.name: O2 penetration depth, gas-phase supply through air-filled pores
parameters.source_title: Diffusion in Biofilms
parameters.notes: Same zero-order slab formula, gas-phase inputs: C_0 = C_O2_gas = 8.42 mol m-3 (30 C), D_eff = D_O2_gas_eff (Millington-Quirk on air-filled porosity), R = R_O2_bulk. Evaluated: Sw=0.3: R_lo -> 513 mm, R_hi -> 100 mm. Sw=0.4: 397 / 77 mm. Sw=0.5: 293 / 57 mm. Sw=0.6: 202 / 39 mm. Sw=0.7: 125 / 24 mm. Sw=0.8: 64 / 12 mm. VALUE = Sw=0.5 with R_hi = 57 mm; low = the pessimistic corner (Sw=0.8, R_hi) = 12 mm; high = the optimistic corner (Sw=0.3, R_lo) = 513 mm. DESIGN USE: for the CMU-scale wall thicknesses in the brief (face shell ~32 mm, web ~25 mm) even the pessimistic 12 mm one-sided depth covers a 25 mm web exposed on BOTH faces (2 x 12 = 24 mm), which is exactly why the split-mould two-half casting works. A solid 20x20x40 cm block cast in one piece is 100 mm from any surface to its centre and fails at every corner of this range. Treat 2*L_O2_gas as the maximum admissible wall thickness and sample Sw, since Sw is what the drying schedule controls.

parameters.name: Viable cell density of inoculum suspension
parameters.source_title: Reinforcement of Different Sands by Low-pH Bio-Mineralization
parameters.notes: Lai et al. 2023 used three suspension concentrations: 0.67e8, 3e8 and 10e8 cells/mL. ORGANISM MISMATCH: S. pasteurii, ureolytic. The count is nonetheless usable for B. subtilis because it is a suspension-density figure set by culture practice, not by the metabolic pathway. The paper's own OD600-to-count conversion (their Eq. 6) is Y = 8.59e7 * Z^1.3627 with Y in cells/mL and Z = OD600 — they measured OD600 1.7-1.8 after 48 h and reported ~1e8 cells/mL. Cross-checks in other retrieved work: Konstantinou et al. 2021 (10.1038/s41598-021-85712-6) worked at OD600 = 2 and 3; Ebigbo et al. 2012 (10.1029/2011wr011714) Table 1 injected inocula of 1.3e7 to 4.0e9 cfu/mL across four columns [see OCR CAVEAT below]; Fu et al. 2023 (10.1016/j.bgtech.2023.100002) report ureolysis rate correlating linearly with log cell concentration over 1e6 to 1e8 cells/mL. IMPORTANT COUNTER-FINDING: higher is not better — Lai et al. found the effective reinforcement DEPTH increases as bacterial concentration DECREASES, and Fu et al. note high bacterial concentrations clog pores and prevent free flow. OCR CAVEAT ON THE EBIGBO FIGURES: that table was read from PDF text extraction in which decimal points came through as colons, so the four biomass entries appear as '14:0 x 10^9', '21:1 x 10^8', '36:5 x 10^8', '41:3 x 10^7'. These are SEVEN-FIELD rows in which the LEADING DIGIT IS THE COLUMN INDEX, not part of the mantissa: stripping it yields column numbers 1,2,3,4 in sequence and mantissas 4.0, 1.1, 6.5, 1.3, giving 4.0e9, 1.1e8, 6.5e8, 1.3e7 cfu/mL and hence the 1.3e7-4.0e9 range quoted above. Two independent checks confirm that alignment: (i) the recovered column indices are exactly 1,2,3,4 in order, which no alternative parse reproduces; (ii) column 1 carries the most Ca2+ pulses (35) and is the only row with 'no' in the rinse-influent field, matching the paper's narrative that column 1 clogged near the injection point and columns 2-4 used the modified rinse-first strategy. An alternative parse reading the entries as 1.40e9/2.11e8/3.65e8/4.13e7 was considered and REJECTED: it leaves the Column field unfilled and requires shifting the decimal two places, whereas a colon-for-decimal-point substitution on '14:0' gives 14.0, not 1.40. NOTE ALSO that this row's value/low/high come from Lai et al. 2023 (full text retrieved), NOT from the Ebigbo table, so the OCR question never affected any numeric field here.

parameters.name: OD600 of inoculum at treatment
parameters.source_title: The role of bacterial urease activity on the uniformity of carbonate precipitation profiles of bio-treated coarse sand specimens
parameters.notes: Konstantinou et al. grew cultures to OD600 = 1 for the generational programme and ran the coarse-sand column experiments at OD600 = 2 and 3, having rejected OD600 = 0.1 (crystals form slowly, larger, fewer) and noting that at OD600 = 3 precipitation increased but large amounts of unstable CaCO3 polymorphs appeared. For the non-ureolytic B. subtilis route, Hemayati et al. 2023 (10.1038/s41598-023-33070-w) optimised over OD 0.5 / 1 / 1.5 and found increasing bacterial concentration beyond OD = 1 gave no appreciable extra CaCO3 — so for OUR organism and pathway the useful setpoint is OD600 ~ 1, at the low end of this row. Do not convert OD600 to cells/mL with a generic factor: Beal et al. 2020 (10.1038/s42003-020-01127-5) show OD is a light-scatter quantity that is not comparable between instruments without a bead calibration and is not even linear in cell count outside a limited range.

parameters.name: Effective cementation depth, surface percolation into FINE sand (<0.3 mm)
parameters.substrate: fine sand (<0.3 mm), 2 m columns and 3-D trials
parameters.source_title: Upscaling Effects of Soil Improvement by Microbially Induced Calcite Precipitation by Surface Percolation
parameters.notes:
Cheng & Cord-Ruwisch 2014, the canonical surface-percolation depth-limit result. In 2 m one-dimensional fine-sand (<0.3 mm) columns, repeated treatments caused CLOGGING AT THE INJECTION END, giving 'limited cementation depth of less than 1 m' (high bound). In the three-dimensional fine-sand trials, relatively homogeneous cementation was achieved with 80% of the sand cemented to 2-2.5 MPa 'to a depth of 20 cm' (value / low bound). Their mathematical model attributes cementation depth to the competition between infiltration rate of the cementation solution and in-situ urease activity, and correctly predicted that repeated treatments enhance clogging near the injection point. ORGANISM MISMATCH: ureolytic S. pasteurii, whose fast urea hydrolysis is precisely what drives near-surface clogging. B. subtilis non-ureolytic MICP is slower, so the clogging front should be less abrupt — but there is no B. subtilis measurement of this, so DO NOT transfer the number as-is. For B. subtilis, the O2-limited depth (L_O2_gas) is likely to bind before the clogging depth does.

parameters.name: Effective reinforcement depth, single spray/percolation treatment (surface crust)
parameters.substrate: quartz / calcareous / tailings / reclaimed sand, sprayed
parameters.source_title: Reinforcement of Different Sands by Low-pH Bio-Mineralization
parameters.notes: Two independent lines. (1) Lai et al. 2023 measured effective reinforcement depth by micro-penetration (depth of the penetration-resistance peak) on sprayed samples in culture dishes 95 mm dia x 16 mm high and syringe moulds, at 0.5 pore-volume spray, porosity 0.69; they report DIFFERENCES between sands of 4-10 mm, which bounds the absolute depths at the same order (single-digit to low-tens of mm) and gives the low bound of 6 mm. parameters.name: Effective treatment radius / uniform depth under pressurised grouting
parameters.source_title: Large-scale experimental investigation of biotreated sand column using different grouting pipe configurations
parameters.notes:

Included because it is the clearest recent demonstration that even with active pumping the uniformly-treated dimension is decimetres, not metres. Not directly transferable to gravity/spray casting; use as an upper sanity bound on how large a monolith can be treated uniformly by any delivery method.

parameters.name: Cementation non-uniformity: CaCO3 top-to-bottom gradient under fast reaction
parameters.substrate: very coarse sand, 70 mm dia x 150 mm specimens
parameters.source_title: The role of bacterial urease activity on the uniformity of carbonate precipitation profiles of bio-treated coarse sand specimens
parameters.notes: Konstantinou et al. 2021: with HIGH urease activity 'the distribution of the cementation was highly uneven', CaCO3 'tended to be high at the top of the specimens and low or nil at the bottom' over a specimen only 150 mm tall. Lowering urease activity gave progressively more uniform samples and the paper concludes it is 'effective enough when its value is less than 10 mmol/L/h' (their activity levels spanned 0.45 to 294 mmol/L/h). No scalar value is given here because the finding is a threshold on REACTION RATE, not a length. RELEVANCE TO OUR ORGANISM: this is the strongest argument that B. subtilis being a SLOW carbonate producer is an advantage for uniformity, not merely a handicap — the whole thrust of the MICP uniformity literature (this paper; low-pH injection in Lai et al. 10.3390/ma16186211; low-temperature dual inhibition in Huang et al. 10.3390/ma18112514) is deliberately slowing the reaction down to get uniform, deeply-penetrating cementation.

parameters.name: Cementation solution molarity, UREOLYTIC route (CaCl2; urea reported separately)
parameters.units: mol L-1 CaCl2 (urea is NOT equal to this value: see C_urea_ureolytic row)
parameters.source_title: The role of bacterial urease activity on the uniformity of carbonate precipitation profiles of bio-treated coarse sand specimens
parameters.notes: UNITS CORRECTION: an earlier version of this file labelled the units '(each of CaCl2 and urea)', which misstated the source. Konstantinou et al. used 0.375 M UREA + 0.25 M CaCl2 + 3 g/L nutrient broth: the two are DELIBERATELY UNEQUAL, and the paper states that a urea:calcium ratio greater than one is recommended (0.375/0.25 = 1.5 here). This row is the CaCl2 concentration only; the urea concentration is carried in its own row. The paper describes the recipe as 'consistent with several previous studies that showed effective MICP treatment'. Upper bound 1.0 M from Fu et al. 2023 (10.1016/j.bgtech.2023.100002), which cites Al Qabany & Soga: 1 mol/L caused EARLY permeability reduction (clogging) whereas 0.25 and 0.5 mol/L gave gradual reduction. Fu et al. also give the combined metric: for OD600 0.8-1.2 an input rate of 0.042 mol/L corresponds to injection intervals of 6, 12 or 24 h at 0.25, 0.5 or 1 mol/L respectively. LISTED FOR REFERENCE ONLY: this is the ureolytic pathway. Our organism is non-ureolytic B. subtilis, which uses NO urea at all: see C_Ca_nonureolytic, which is the row the model should use.

parameters.name: Urea concentration, UREOLYTIC route (reference only, not used by our pathway)
parameters.source_title: The role of bacterial urease activity on the uniformity of carbonate precipitation profiles of bio-treated coarse sand specimens
parameters.notes: Split out from the former combined row to remove an incorrect units annotation. Konstantinou et al. used 0.375 M urea against 0.25 M CaCl2, i.e. a urea:calcium molar ratio of 1.5, and note that a ratio greater than one is recommended because it enhances ureolysis and precipitation rates. High bound 1.0 M reflects the 1 M urea + 1 M CaCl2 recipe used as the ureolytic CONTROL by Hemayati et al. 2023 (10.1038/s41598-023-33070-w). ZERO FOR OUR PROCESS: the non-ureolytic B. subtilis route produces carbonate by aerobic oxidation of formate/acetate and adds no urea, which is precisely why it emits no ammonia. Retained only so the model can reproduce ureolytic benchmarks for comparison.

parameters.name: Calcium source concentration, NON-UREOLYTIC aerobic route (B. subtilis)
parameters.source_title: New non-ureolytic heterotrophic microbial induced carbonate precipitation for suppression of sand dune wind erosion
parameters.notes: THE KEY OUR-ORGANISM, OUR-PATHWAY PROTOCOL ROW. Hemayati et al. 2023 optimised non-ureolytic MICP with B. subtilis (PTCC, ATCC-derived) on calcium FORMATE and calcium ACETATE, no urea and no ammonia by-product. Optimisation levels for calcium-source concentration were 10, 30, 50 g/L and the paper states CaCO3 production increased monotonically with concentration, so 50 g/L is the optimum within the tested range (value = high = 50 g/L; low = 10 g/L is the lowest level tested). Molarity conversion for the model: calcium formate Ca(HCOO)2 M = 130.1 g/mol -> 50 g/L = 0.384 M; calcium acetate Ca(CH3COO)2 M = 158.2 g/mol -> 50 g/L = 0.316 M (DERIVED arithmetic, formula weights are standard). Note these molarities land in the same 0.25-0.5 M window the ureolytic literature converged on, which is a useful consistency check. Other optimised factors from the same study: OD = 1 (no benefit beyond), calcium-source-to-bacterial-solution volume ratio = 1, initial culture pH = 9 for B. subtilis (its growth optimum pH range is 7-9 and the CoA enzyme optimum is 8-9.2), curing 9 days at 30 C. CALCIUM FORMATE OUTPERFORMED ACETATE and B. subtilis outperformed B. amyloliquefaciens; the best composition produced roughly three times the CaCO3 of the worst.

parameters.name: Number of treatment cycles to reach a self-supporting solid
parameters.source_title: Manufacturing bio-bricks using microbial induced calcium carbonate precipitation and human urine
parameters.notes: Spread across the retrieved protocols, and it is genuinely wide. Lambert & Randall 2019 needed 48 treatment cycles over 4 days to reach 2.7 MPa in a full-size brick mould (222 x 106 x 73 mm, pore volume 650 mL), with 2 h minimum retention time per cycle (high bound). Konstantinou et al. 2021 (10.1038/s41598-021-85712-6) administered 15 injections at 24 h intervals (value). Huang et al. 2025 (10.3390/ma18112514) reached UCS 2.5 MPa after FOUR treatment cycles using low-temperature dual inhibition (low bound). Ugur et al. 2024 (10.1021/acsami.3c13971) showed that pre-trapping bacteria on the sand with an aminosilane cut the requirement from 7 injections to 3 for the same strength — i.e. cycle count is a function of how well bacteria are retained, not a material constant. ORGANISM MISMATCH: all ureolytic and therefore fast; expect B. subtilis non-ureolytic to need MORE cycles or longer ones. For the non-ureolytic case Hemayati et al. (10.1038/s41598-023-33070-w) used a SINGLE spray application at 1-3 L/m2 followed by 9 days curing — a different protocol shape entirely (few cycles, long cure) that is probably the better template for our organism.

parameters.name: Interval between treatment cycles
parameters.source_title: The role of bacterial urease activity on the uniformity of carbonate precipitation profiles of bio-treated coarse sand specimens
parameters.notes: Konstantinou et al. used a 24 h retention time between successive injections for both bacterial and cementation injections (value / high), reasoning that low chemical concentrations or long retention times are needed for reactions to complete throughout the specimen 'even at the remotest places'. Lambert & Randall 2019 found the minimum workable retention time was 2 h (low bound) and that calcium efficiency stayed above 97% for retention times of 2-8 h. Fu et al. 2023 (10.1016/j.bgtech.2023.100002) synthesise the trade-off: 24 h intervals give large rhombohedral calcite whereas short 3-5 h intervals give numerous small spherical crystals, and longer intervals improved both chemical efficiency and strength. LONGER IS BETTER for uniformity and efficiency; shorter only helps throughput.

parameters.name: Curing time
parameters.source_title: New non-ureolytic heterotrophic microbial induced carbonate precipitation for suppression of sand dune wind erosion
parameters.notes: OUR-ORGANISM VALUE. Hemayati et al. 2023 optimised curing time over 3, 6 and 9 days and identified 9 days as the optimum for B. subtilis: for the acetate compositions CaCO3 'increased incessantly until 9 days after which there was little change'. The kinetics differ by calcium source — in the formate + B. subtilis composition 87% of total CaCO3 was already produced after 3 days, versus only ~45% for the acetate + B. subtilis composition. So: 3 days gets most of the yield on formate, 9 days is needed on acetate. Low bound 4 days is Lambert & Randall's 48-cycle / 4-day ureolytic brick schedule, included to show that a fast ureolytic protocol reaches strength in a comparable wall-clock time by cycling harder. For a hollow living artefact fed by dropper (per the design brief) the practical cure is open-ended; 9 days is the point of diminishing CaCO3 return.

parameters.name: Curing / incubation temperature optimum for B. subtilis MICP
parameters.source_title: New non-ureolytic heterotrophic microbial induced carbonate precipitation for suppression of sand dune wind erosion
parameters.notes: Hemayati et al. cultured B. subtilis at 30 C / 180 rpm, cured the MICP solution at 30 C / 220 rpm, and incubated the treated sand dunes at 30 C for the 9-day cure — 30 C is therefore the demonstrated non-ureolytic B. subtilis MICP temperature (value). Bracketing evidence: Hu et al. 2017 (10.1186/s12934-017-0764-z) ran B. subtilis bioreactors at 37 C, the standard laboratory optimum (high bound). Ferral-Perez et al. 2020 (10.1186/s13568-020-01111-6) demonstrated B. subtilis 168 CaCO3 precipitation on calcium acetate and calcium lactate agars (the coupled calcium-carbon sources directly relevant to our route). For the ureolytic literature Fu et al. 2023 note most experiments run near 20 C and that S. pasteurii growth and urease optimum is 25-30 C (low bound 25 C). PRACTICAL NOTE: 30 C also sits below the 40 C ceiling above which urea decomposes chemically (Lambert & Randall 2019) — irrelevant for our urea-free route but relevant if the team ever benchmarks against urea.

parameters.name: CaCO3 yield per treatment cycle (% by mass of aggregate)
parameters.units: % by mass of dry aggregate per cycle
parameters.source_title: Manufacturing bio-bricks using microbial induced calcium carbonate precipitation and human urine
parameters.notes: KEY DERIVED ROW — no retrieved paper reports %/cycle directly, so it is computed two ways. (A) From Lambert & Randall 2019: brick mould 0.222 x 0.106 x 0.073 m = 1.718 L; measured pore volume 650 mL implies porosity 650e-6/1.718e-3 = 0.378; sand mass = 1.718e-3 * (1-0.378) * 2650 kg/m3 = 2.830 kg (grain density 2650 kg/m3 ASSUMED, standard for quartz). Influent Ca 0.09-0.13 M with reported calcium usage efficiency ~98%: at 0.09 M, n = 0.09*0.650*0.98 = 0.0573 mol -> 5.74 g CaCO3 (M = 100.09 g/mol) -> 5.74/2830 = 0.203 %/cycle; at 0.13 M -> 8.29 g -> 0.293 %/cycle. Over their 48 cycles that integrates to 9.7-14.1 % by mass, consistent with the 2.7 MPa they measured. (B) From Konstantinou et al. 2021: specimen 70 mm dia x 150 mm = 0.577 L, porosity 0.40 (ASSUMED, not stated in the extracted text) -> pore volume 0.231 L, sand 0.918 kg; 0.25 M CaCl2 at 1.1 pore volumes per injection = 0.0635 mol Ca delivered; at their reported ~50% chemical efficiency -> 3.18 g -> 0.346 %/cycle, at 100% -> 0.692 %/cycle (high bound). value = 0.20 %/cycle, the best-constrained (route A, lowest Ca) figure. CONTEXT FOR THE SUCCESS CRITERION: Fu et al. 2023 (10.1016/j.bgtech.2023.100002) report that a specimen needs a minimum CaCO3 content of circa 3% to stand alone unconfined for a UCS test, that UCS spans <50 kPa to >18 MPa over CaCO3 contents from <1% to >35% with a NONLINEAR (accelerating) relationship, and that under confinement <2% often suffices. At 0.2-0.7 %/cycle, reaching the 3% self-supporting threshold needs roughly 4-15 cycles.

parameters.name: CaCO3 content achieved by single-application non-ureolytic B. subtilis spray
parameters.substrate: sand dune surface, 2 L/m2, 1 cycle, 9 d cure at 30 C
parameters.source_title: New non-ureolytic heterotrophic microbial induced carbonate precipitation for suppression of sand dune wind erosion
parameters.notes: OUR-ORGANISM, OUR-PATHWAY YIELD. Hemayati et al. Table 2: B. subtilis + calcium FORMATE at 2 L/m2 application rate, one MICP cycle -> surface resistance 190 kPa and calcium carbonate content 2.8% (value/high); B. subtilis + calcium ACETATE, same rate and cycle -> 150 kPa and 1.3% (low). Their ureolytic S. pasteurii control at 2 L/m2 gave 132 kPa and 2.41% — SO THE NON-UREOLYTIC B. SUBTILIS FORMATE ROUTE ACTUALLY EXCEEDED THE UREOLYTIC CONTROL on both metrics in this study, which materially weakens the usual assumption that B. subtilis is simply a weaker substitute. Caveat: this is a thin sprayed surface crust on a dune, not a cast monolith, and the resistances (150-190 kPa) are two orders below the 2.5-2.7 MPa that multi-cycle ureolytic column/brick protocols reach. The polymorph was vaterite (spherical, 'lettuce-like'), not calcite — vaterite is the metastable phase, which raises a durability question the paper does not resolve.

parameters.name: Curing relative humidity
parameters.notes: NO RETRIEVED SOURCE gives a measured optimal curing RH for biocemented granular composites. This is the largest outright gap in the parameter set and the row is honestly ASSUMED with no DOI. What the retrieved literature does establish, qualitatively: the design brief itself reports cracking and incomplete mineralisation from UNEVEN DRYING and that the successful split-mould protocol used humidity control; Hemayati et al. cured in a closed incubator at 30 C (RH not reported); Lambert & Randall's bio-brick system was deliberately CLOSED to avoid ammonia volatilisation, i.e. effectively saturated; Wang et al. 2015 (10.3389/fmicb.2015.01088) kept mortar prisms in a moisture room for 28 days and used dynamic vapour sorption across a range of RHs to argue that moisture uptake capacity governs whether a bacteria-based healing system stays active. 90-100% RH is the standard cementitious-curing convention and is adopted here on that basis. THE CONFLICT THE MODEL MUST RESOLVE: high RH keeps cells alive and hydrated but keeps pore saturation high, which is exactly what collapses the gas-phase O2 supply (see D_O2_gas_eff and L_O2_gas). RH should not be treated as a free parameter to maximise — it trades directly against oxygenation.

parameters.name: Evaporation rate at onset of diffusion-limited (stage-2) drying in sand
parameters.substrate: sands and glass beads of different particle size distributions
parameters.source_title: What determines drying rates at the onset of diffusion controlled stage‐2 evaporation from porous media?
parameters.notes:
Shokri & Or 2011 report that the range of evaporation rates at the onset of stage-2 evaporation is 'relatively narrow (0.5-2.5 mm d-1)' across their sand and glass-bead experiments plus literature data; value = 1.5 mm/d is the midpoint. PHYSICAL MEANING AND WHY IT MATTERS FOR CRACKING: during stage-1 the drying front stays hydraulically connected to the surface by capillary flow and drying is quasi-uniform; at the onset of stage-2 the connection breaks, the vaporisation plane JUMPS to a depth below the surface, and drying becomes vapour-diffusion-limited and depth-nonuniform. Their jump length follows a power law in Bond number with exponent -0.48, matching the percolation-theory value -0.47. DESIGN INTERPRETATION (an inference, not the paper's claim): holding the imposed drying rate AT OR BELOW this range keeps the casting in the uniform stage-1 regime for as long as possible, which is the transport-physics reading of the brief's 'uneven drying' failure mode. No paper in this retrieval measured a critical drying rate for CRACK INITIATION in a biocemented granular composite — that number does not appear to exist yet.

parameters.name: Relative effective diffusivity of O2 inside biofilm (De/Daq)
parameters.source_title: Diffusion in Biofilms
parameters.notes: Stewart 2003: De/Daq in biofilm 'ranges from ca. 0.2 to 0.8 with a mean value of ca. 0.4', the author recommends 0.6 for light gases (O2, CO2, N2O, CH4) and 0.25 for most organic solutes, and the paper's own O2 example uses the Fig. 1 consensus value 0.57 for oxygen specifically (value). Needed as a SECOND resistance in series if the model resolves diffusion into the biofilm itself rather than treating the biofilm as a lumped sink; for a pore-scale model where biofilm occupies only 1-10% of pore space it is a minor correction compared with the granular tortuosity term. Note the useful asymmetry: gases pass biofilm relatively freely (0.57-0.6) while the ORGANIC CARBON SOURCE our non-ureolytic route depends on is hindered ~2x more (0.25).

parameters.name: Aqueous diffusivities of nutrient / carbon-source solutes at 25 C
parameters.source_title: Diffusion in Biofilms
parameters.notes: Stewart 2003 Table 1, diffusion coefficients in water at 25 C, in units of 1e-6 cm2/s (multiply by 1e-10 for m2/s): oxygen 20.0, carbon dioxide 19.2, urea 13.8, acetic acid 12.1, formic acid 14.1, glycerol 9.4, glucose 6.7, sucrose 5.2, bicarbonate HCO3- 11.8, ammonium NH4+ 19.7, chloride 20.3, sulfate 10.6. FOR OUR NON-UREOLYTIC ROUTE the operative numbers are acetate/formate as the carbon source (12.1 and 14.1 -> 1.21e-9 and 1.41e-9 m2/s) and bicarbonate as the carbonate carrier (11.8 -> 1.18e-9 m2/s). Apply the same tortuosity correction as for dissolved O2 (a_MQ / Archie / Boudreau rows) and the biofilm factor 0.25 for organics from f_biofilm. CRITICAL COMPARISON: acetate at 1.21e-9 m2/s diffuses at 60% of the dissolved-O2 rate but is supplied at 300-400 mM (50 g/L calcium acetate = 0.316 M) versus O2 at 0.24 mM. The molar supply ratio is ~1300:1 in favour of the carbon source, so for the aerobic non-ureolytic pathway OXYGEN IS THE LIMITING REACTANT BY A LARGE MARGIN, not the carbon source or the calcium. This row exists mainly to establish that conclusion quantitatively.

parameters.name: Initial porosity of packed granular medium
parameters.substrate: quartz sand column / brick mould / loose sprayed sand
parameters.source_title: Darcy‐scale modeling of microbially induced carbonate mineral precipitation in sand columns
parameters.notes: Ebigbo et al. 2012 Table 3: measured initial porosity 0.40 for their sand columns, with initial permeabilities 1.79e-8 to 2.30e-8 dm2 (value). Lambert & Randall's brick mould implies 0.378 (650 mL pore volume in a 1.718 L mould; low bound). Lai et al. 2023 (10.3390/ma16186211) report porosity 0.69 for sand compacted to only 85% of maximum dry density in shallow spray moulds (high bound) — very loose. Used throughout the derivations above at 0.40. The brief's ground construction waste is a broadly graded crushed material with d_max up to 4 mm; its packing porosity has NOT been measured and could sit anywhere in this range, so it should be sampled. It matters twice: it sets the tortuosity correction (phi^2 denominator) and it sets the aggregate mass per unit volume that fixes CaCO3 %.

parameters.name: Calcite (CaCO3) crystal density
parameters.source_title: Darcy‐scale modeling of microbially induced carbonate mineral precipitation in sand columns
parameters.notes: Ebigbo et al. 2012 Table 3 lists calcite density rho_c = 2710 g L-1 = 2710 kg m-3, used by them to convert ICP-MS calcium measurements into a calcite volume fraction phi_c. Needed to convert the CaCO3 mass percentages in this table into the pore-volume occupancy that drives permeability loss and clogging in the model.

parameters.name: Bacterial retention (attachment + straining) in saturated sand, single pass
parameters.source_title: Transport and Fate of Ureolytic Sporosarcina pasteurii in Saturated Sand Columns: Experiments and Modelling
parameters.notes: Sang et al. 2023 column breakthrough experiments with a two-site kinetic model separating ATTACHMENT on grain surfaces from STRAINING at crevices and constrictions. Reported: raising ionic strength 0.5 -> 1000 mM raised attachment 9.4% -> 69.6% and straining 8.1% -> 34.2%; raising flow velocity 50 -> 200 cm/h LOWERED attachment 39.5% -> 22.4% and straining 40.5% -> 19.3%; lowering initial OD600 1.0 -> 0.48 RAISED attachment 31.8% -> 40.9% and straining 22.9% -> 42.2% by relieving site blockage. Retention = attachment + straining: low bound 9.4+8.1 = 17.5% (low ionic strength), high bound 69.6+34.2 = 103.8% (capped at ~100% in practice; the two figures come from different runs), value ~55% as a mid-range. ORGANISM MISMATCH: S. pasteurii. DESIGN LEVERS THIS EXPOSES: 0.5 M CaCl2 increased retention while deionised water caused release, and slow infiltration retains far more cells than fast — both directly controllable in a spray/percolation casting protocol.

parameters.name: B. subtilis oxygen requirement: growth without O2 as terminal electron acceptor
parameters.source_title: ANAEROBIC GROWTH OF A “STRICT AEROBE” (BACILLUS SUBTILIS)
parameters.notes:
IMPORTANT CORRECTION TO A PREMISE IN THE DESIGN BRIEF. The brief states B. subtilis 'cannot grow without O2 as terminal electron acceptor'. Nakano & Zuber 1998 review exactly this: 'There was a long-held belief that the gram-positive soil bacterium Bacillus subtilis is a strict aerobe. But recent studies have shown that B. subtilis will grow anaerobically, either by using nitrate or nitrite as a terminal electron acceptor, or by fermentation.' The ResD/ResE two-component system induces fnr on oxygen limitation, and FNR activates the respiratory nitrate reductase narGHJI. PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE: strict anoxia is survivable but NOT USEFUL for our purpose, because the non-ureolytic MICP pathway itself is oxidative — Hemayati et al. (10.1038/s41598-023-33070-w) precipitate CaCO3 by AEROBIC OXIDATION of formate/acetate (HCOO- + O2 -> CO2 + H2O, then CO2 + H2O <-> HCO3- <-> CO3^2- and Ca2+ + CO3^2- -> CaCO3). No O2 means no CO2 means no carbonate. So the aerobic geometric constraint stands on stoichiometric grounds even though the organism is not literally an obligate aerobe. A nitrate-respiring fallback would need a different carbonate-generating chemistry and is out of scope of anything retrieved here.

PROVENANCE LIMIT (added at audit): the primary source was NOT opened in this session. fetch_article_fulltext returned found:false for this DOI (publisher paywall; no OA copy via Unpaywall, Semantic Scholar, PMC or CrossRef TDM). The quoted sentence and the ResD/ResE-FNR/narGHJI mechanism were read from the PubMed abstract, which states them verbatim. Evidence label moved MEASURED -> SECONDARY. The stoichiometric argument that follows (no O2 -> no CO2 -> no carbonate) rests on Hemayati et al. 2023, whose full text WAS retrieved and whose reaction scheme is quoted there.

parameters.name: MICP strength penalty under oxygen restriction
parameters.units: fold reduction in UCS (aerated vs air-restricted)
parameters.source_title: Impact of Oxygen Availability on Microbially Induced Calcite Precipitation (MICP) Treatment
parameters.notes:
Li et al. 2017 ran matched MICP treatments under aerated, open-air and air-restricted conditions. Dissolved oxygen in the air-restricted reactor 'decreased with time and was almost exhausted within 7 days'; in the open box DO fell 50% over 7 days from superficial air supply only; in the aerated box DO stayed at its initial high level. UCS and CaCO3 content were high (aerated) / moderate (open) / poor (air-restricted), and the paper states 'The UCS can be 100 times different depending on the different oxygen supply conditions'. ORGANISM MISMATCH: S. pasteurii, and note the twist — the review by Fu et al. 2023 records that S. pasteurii urease can remain ACTIVE under anoxia because the enzyme was made earlier during aerobic culture, so a ureolytic system is partly buffered against O2 loss in a way our non-ureolytic system is NOT. For B. subtilis the aerobic oxidation IS the carbonate-generating step, so a 100-fold penalty is if anything a conservative transfer. This is the strongest quantitative justification in the literature for treating oxygen supply as the primary geometric driver, as the design brief already concluded qualitatively.

PROVENANCE LIMIT (added at audit): the primary source was NOT opened in this session. fetch_article_fulltext returned found:false for this DOI (publisher paywall; no OA copy via Unpaywall, Semantic Scholar, PMC or CrossRef TDM). The 100-fold UCS figure and the three DO regimes were read from the publisher abstract retrieved via OpenAlex, which states them verbatim ('The UCS can be 100 times different depending on the different oxygen supply conditions'). CORROBORATION FROM A FULLY-RETRIEVED SOURCE: Fu et al. 2023 (10.1016/j.bgtech.2023.100002), full text opened, cites this work as reference [141] and reports that at equal 7-day treatment duration, air-restricted samples were substantially weaker than aerated ones.
